**Memory requirements** (measured by compiling with an ESP32, values rounded up):
- Progmem: 225'000
- Dynamic memory: 14'000

**Supported platforms:** The page says SAM is written in C and "runs on most popular platforms," and it is designed to work on embedded computers. The Arduino library specifically targets Arduino-compatible boards. The only named platform in the memory measurements is the ESP32.

**Sample rate:** 22050 Hz, 16 bits per sample, 1 channel (mono). You can switch to 2 channels with `sam.setOutputChannels(2);`.

**License:** The page gives no open source license. It says the software is a reverse-engineered version of a commercial product, and the copyright holder is SoftVoice, Inc. It states: "we cannot put the code under any specific open source software license." The author describes the software as abandonware and says to "Use it at your own risk."

**Quality notes:** The page does not give a quality rating or listening assessment. It does include:
- It is an adaptation of the 1982 Commodore 64 SAM speech software, which includes a text-to-phoneme converter ("reciter") and a phoneme-to-speech routine.
- Six voice presets (Elf, Little Robot, Stuffy Guy, Little Old Lady, Extra-Terrestrial, SAM) that adjust speed, pitch, throat, and mouth parameters.
- A link to an external site for trying alternative parameter combinations.

194	 * app too (app_ble_scan_report, main loop; pdu: the advertising PDU, its 2-byte header, AdvA and data, n bytes; rssi:
195	 * the radio's reading), plat_ble_connect_peer connects to one by its address with the bond the app kept, and the keys
196	 * a pairing with it gave come to the app (app_ble_device_keys, main loop). The state is
197	 * plat_ble_device's; the bytes are least significant first, as on the air. ble_central = 3: the central without pairing
198	 * (no keys, no passkey; a device that asks for security fails with PLAT_BLE_CF_NEED_PAIR) */
199	struct plat_ble_peer {
200	    uint8_t addr[6], addr_rand;        /* its address as heard (addr_rand: TxAdd, a random one) */
201	    uint8_t bonded;                    /* ltk / rand / ediv are its bond: the link is encrypted with them */
202	    uint8_t sec;                       /* PLAT_BLE_PEER_* */
203	    uint8_t ltk[16], rand[8];
204	    uint16_t ediv;
205	};
206	#define PLAT_BLE_PEER_AUTH 1u          /* its bond is authenticated (a passkey pairing) */
207	#define PLAT_BLE_PEER_MITM 2u          /* it needs an authenticated link: a pairing goes straight to the passkey */
208	struct plat_ble_keys {
209	    uint8_t has;                       /* PLAT_BLE_KEYS_* */
210	    uint8_t ltk[16], rand[8];
211	    uint16_t ediv;
212	    uint8_t irk[16], id[6], id_rand;   /* its identity: behind a private address, plat_ble_rpa_resolve finds it */
213	};
214	#define PLAT_BLE_KEYS_LTK 1u           /* ltk / rand / ediv: the bond */
215	#define PLAT_BLE_KEYS_ID 2u            /* irk / id / id_rand */
216	#define PLAT_BLE_KEYS_AUTH 4u          /* the pairing was authenticated (a passkey) */
217	enum { PLAT_BLE_CF_NONE, PLAT_BLE_CF_LOST, PLAT_BLE_CF_NO_MIDI, PLAT_BLE_CF_PAIRING, PLAT_BLE_CF_AUTH, PLAT_BLE_CF_GATT,
218	       PLAT_BLE_CF_NEED_MITM, PLAT_BLE_CF_KEY, PLAT_BLE_CF_NEED_PAIR };   /* why a connection to a device ended: lost,
219	                                        * no MIDI found, the pairing failed, the encryption refused, the GATT failed, it
220	                                        * needs a passkey (connect again with PLAT_BLE_PEER_MITM, no unauthenticated
221	                                        * bond), it refused our bond, it asked for security (ble_central = 3) */
222	#define PLAT_BLE_DF_PAIRING 1u         /* plat_ble_device_flags: a pairing of ours runs on the link */
223	#define PLAT_BLE_DF_PROMPTED 2u        /* one started on the last attempt's link (its user was asked) */
224	#define PLAT_BLE_DF_MITM 4u            /* the last attempt's device needs an authenticated link (a passkey) */
225	int plat_ble_connect_peer(const struct plat_ble_peer *p);   /* 0 = connecting (plat_ble_device), -1 not now */
226	int plat_ble_device_fail(uint32_t *code);   /* why the last connection to a device ended (PLAT_BLE_CF_*); code: its
227	                                        * code (the link layer's reason, the ATT error or the SMP reason) */
228	uint32_t plat_ble_device_flags(void);  /* PLAT_BLE_DF_* */
229	int plat_ble_rpa_resolve(const uint8_t irk[16], const uint8_t addr[6]);   /* 1: addr is a private address made from irk */
230	void app_ble_scan_report(const uint8_t *pdu, uint32_t n, uint32_t rssi);
231	void app_ble_device_keys(const struct plat_ble_keys *k);
232	/* Bluetooth on or off, as the player asks: off ends every link, stops advertising and scanning (the radio quiet);
233	 * on starts it (or advertises again). Whether it starts at power-on: APP_BLE_AT_BOOT (app.h, e.g. a saved setting;
234	 * default 1) */
235	void plat_ble_enable(int on);
236	/* What Bluetooth keeps (the own stack, ble_stack = "own"), by default in the app's store object OBJ_BLE. An app that
237	 * keeps it in its own saved data instead (a settings record it has, with these fields at its own places) defines
238	 * APP_BLE_STORE in app.h and gives the two calls below; it then needs no OBJ_BLE. app_ble_load: at Bluetooth's start
239	 * (main loop), 1 with r filled, 0 none kept (the platform makes the address then, and saves it); app_ble_save: main
240	 * loop, once something changed (a new address, a pairing, a remembered audio device), 0 kept (the app may write it
241	 * to the flash later, with its own data) */
242	struct plat_ble_rec {
243	    uint8_t addr[6];                   /* our BLE address (static random: the top two bits 1) */
244	    uint8_t bonded, rsv;               /* the computer's bond (ble_pairing): bonded, ediv, rand, ltk */
245	    uint16_t bond_ediv;
246	    uint8_t bond_rand[8], bond_ltk[16];
247	    uint8_t bta_addr[6], bta_addr_set;   /* Bluetooth audio (bt_audio): our BR/EDR address, once made */
248	    uint8_t bta_n;                     /* the remembered audio devices, the last one first */
249	    struct plat_bta_dev {
250	        uint8_t addr[6], bonded, link_key[16];   /* link_key: from its pairing (air order), when bonded */
251	        char name[17];
252	    } bta[4];
253	};
254	int app_ble_load(struct plat_ble_rec *r);
255	int app_ble_save(const struct plat_ble_rec *r);

258	 * and speakers (SBC), beside Bluetooth MIDI on the one radio. While it streams, the render goes to the device and the
259	 * FM-1's own output is muted. Four devices are remembered with their keys (in OBJ_BLE), the last one first. Expect
260	 * 150-300 ms from a key to the ear (the device's own buffer): for listening, not for playing in time. */

265	       PLAT_BTA_STREAMING, PLAT_BTA_REFUSED, PLAT_BTA_NO_LAST, PLAT_BTA_FAILED, PLAT_BTA_READY };

268	                                        * (only when nothing else is under way: a page goes on), 0 stop */

270	int plat_bta_known(int i, char *name); /* remembered device i (0 the last one) -> 0: none */
271	void plat_bta_pick(int i);             /* connect found device i (pairing if new; it becomes the last one) */
272	int plat_bta_reconnect(int i);         /* connect remembered device i -> 0 paging */
273	void plat_bta_forget(int i);
274	void plat_bta_hangup(void);
275	int plat_bta_state(void);              /* PLAT_BTA_* */

278	void plat_bta_output(int to_device);
279	int plat_bta_out_device(void);         /* 1: the sound goes to the device (the default) */
280	/* a link that ended by itself (the device left, or refused): where it had got to, once (then PLAT_BTA_LOST_NONE) */
281	enum { PLAT_BTA_LOST_NONE, PLAT_BTA_LOST_LINK, PLAT_BTA_LOST_PAIRING, PLAT_BTA_LOST_ENCRYPTION, PLAT_BTA_LOST_SETUP,
282	       PLAT_BTA_LOST_STREAMING, PLAT_BTA_LOST_REFUSED };
283	int plat_bta_lost(void);
284	int plat_bta_timed_out(void);          /* PLAT_BTA_REFUSED because the set-up timed out (the device never said no) */
285	int32_t plat_bta_latency_us(void);     /* what the stream adds on the FM-1's side (its queue), us; -1: not streaming.
286	                                        * An app that follows a clock may play that much earlier (the device's own
287	                                        * buffer comes on top and is not known) */
288	/* Bluetooth audio's big buffers in the app's memory (fm1.toml bt_audio_mem = "app": FM1B_BTA_MEM 1): the audio packets'
289	 * queue and the receptions' ring, which only a run of the Classic radio uses (a scan, a page, a link), are a block the
290	 * app lends while an AUDIO mode is on, instead of static RAM: an app that switches Bluetooth audio off has that RAM
291	 * back. Without it (FM1B_BTA_MEM 0) they are static and these say so (bytes 0, the block refused).
292	 *   plat_bta_mem_bytes()  the block's size (4-aligned), 0: static buffers
293	 *   plat_bta_mem(p)       p: the block lent (before plat_bta_on(1), which does nothing without one) -> 0;
294	 *                         0: taken back -> 0 done (the radio's code and interrupts no longer read it), -1 still in use
295	 *                         (an AUDIO mode on, or its run not over yet: plat_bta_on(0) first, then again later) */
296	#ifndef FM1B_BTA_MEM
297	#define FM1B_BTA_MEM 0
298	#endif

302	                                        * render (the audio interrupt) to plan its block by. 0 without Bluetooth audio */

332	/* the 1 kHz tick (app_tick, an app with APP_TICK) runs in the timer interrupt: the main loop locks it out around
333	 * what they share. It nests, and plat_unlock takes what its plat_lock returned: the outermost unlock switches the
334	 * interrupts back on only if they were on at its lock, so a lock is safe inside an interrupt (app_render, app_tick)
335	 * or with them already off: they stay off */
336	uint32_t plat_lock(void);
337	void plat_unlock(uint32_t f);
338	void plat_yield(void);
339	/* the FM-1 restarts, on purpose (an app's own restore done, a session that starts from a clean boot): the sound
340	 * stopped, USB let go (the computer sees the cable out and in), not counted as a failed start (no safe mode), the
341	 * crash record and .noinit kept. Main loop; it does not return (the host simulator: the restart at the end of the
342	 * millisecond, a "reboot"). Built for an app whose app.h defines APP_RESTART */
343	void plat_restart(void);
344	void plat_log(const char *line);
345	/* the flash's data area, 0x97000..0xDFFFF, for an app's own big data (a table it builds, samples): its store objects
346	 * live there too, at the offsets it gave them (APP_STORE_MAP), so it keeps to the rest. Main loop only; an erase or a
347	 * write stops everything for a moment (the sound too: no flash reads meanwhile).
348	 * Two more windows for big data, outside the store: PLAT_XDATA0 (16 KiB, just above the app area) and PLAT_XDATA1
349	 * (92 KiB, above the update's staging). The update loader clears an update record it finds in the last 256 bytes of
350	 * a sector there (bsp/loader/ldr_core.c: "AT" at bytes 0xF06..0xF07, a nonzero CRC-16 at 0xF00 over the 78 bytes
351	 * from 0xF02), so in these two an app keeps bytes 0xF00..0xF07 of every sector erased (0xFF), or else makes sure
352	 * those bytes never read as a record: never "AT" at 0xF06 (LOOM-8's sample bank moves its data so, and refuses a
353	 * bank that has it).
354	 * A fourth, on request (fm1.toml xdata2 = true: FM1B_XDATA2): PLAT_XDATA2, the three sectors 0xFC000..0xFEFFF
355	 * (12 KiB) between the SDK's last area (USR, up to 0xFBFFF) and its key_mac sector (0xFF000, never written), where
356	 * Felucca keeps its globals: an app that was a Felucca firmware reads and writes its own bytes there. The update loader
357	 * looks for records below 0xFC000 only, so no 0xF00 rule here. Store objects may sit there too (the template's
358	 * settings pair is 0xFC000 / 0xFD000): with the window on, plat_data_erase and plat_data_write refuse a store
359	 * object's sectors in it, so an app with this window puts its objects elsewhere (or keeps to the rest) */
360	#define PLAT_DATA_LO 0x97000u
361	#define PLAT_DATA_HI 0xE0000u
362	#define PLAT_XDATA0_LO 0x93000u
363	#define PLAT_XDATA0_HI 0x97000u
364	#define PLAT_XDATA1_LO 0xE5000u
365	#define PLAT_XDATA1_HI 0xFC000u
366	#define PLAT_XDATA2_LO 0xFC000u
367	#define PLAT_XDATA2_HI 0xFF000u
368	#if FM1B_XDATA2
369	#define PLAT_DATA_OK(off, n) (plat_in((off), (n), PLAT_DATA_LO, PLAT_DATA_HI) || \
370	                              plat_in((off), (n), PLAT_XDATA0_LO, PLAT_XDATA0_HI) || \
371	                              plat_in((off), (n), PLAT_XDATA1_LO, PLAT_XDATA1_HI) || \
372	                              plat_in((off), (n), PLAT_XDATA2_LO, PLAT_XDATA2_HI))
373	#else
374	#define PLAT_DATA_OK(off, n) (plat_in((off), (n), PLAT_DATA_LO, PLAT_DATA_HI) || \
375	                              plat_in((off), (n), PLAT_XDATA0_LO, PLAT_XDATA0_HI) || \
376	                              plat_in((off), (n), PLAT_XDATA1_LO, PLAT_XDATA1_HI))
377	#endif
378	static inline int plat_in(uint32_t off, uint32_t n, uint32_t lo, uint32_t hi)   /* [off, off + n) in [lo, hi) */
379	{
380	    return off >= lo && off <= hi && n <= hi - off;
381	}
382	const uint8_t *plat_data(uint32_t off);   /* read in place; 0 = outside the windows */
383	int plat_data_erase(uint32_t off);        /* the 4 KiB sector at off (aligned); 0 = done */
384	int plat_data_write(uint32_t off, const void *src, uint32_t n);   /* src in RAM; 0 = done */
385	/* plat_data_write programs, as NOR flash does: each byte becomes what it was AND what is written (bits go from 1 to
386	 * 0 only, and only an erase sets them again). So it writes into erased flash, and it may also clear bits in place, in
387	 * bytes written before, without an erase: a record's state byte marked used, then dead (0xFF, 0x7F, 0x3F), a bitmap's
388	 * bits taken one by one. Guaranteed on the device (felucca-bsp's fl_write: page program, no erase, no read-back) and
389	 * in the host simulator (the same AND). A 1 written over a 0 stays 0, and is not an error: plat_data_write does not
390	 * read back; an app that must know reads plat_data after. */
391	/* SysEx to the computer over USB (main loop): whole frames, F0 .. F7, into felucca-bsp's SysEx ring (sent before
392	 * the notes), which the USB interrupt empties as the computer reads. plat_sysex_room, plat_sysex_queued and
393	 * plat_usb_session (and plat_sysex_send's -1 without a computer) are built for an app with APP_SYSEX (below) */
394	int plat_sysex_send(const uint8_t *frame, uint32_t n);   /* 0 = queued whole; -1 = not sent: no computer has set
395	                                                         * the FM-1 up (plat_usb_session 0), or it stopped reading
396	                                                         * (no room for 200 ms; what was queued goes out) */
397	uint32_t plat_sysex_room(void);        /* the bytes of SysEx the ring takes now without a wait: 0 with no computer, the
398	                                        * bus asleep, or a send under way. A send that must never wait checks it */
399	uint32_t plat_sysex_queued(void);      /* the bytes still in the ring, not yet read (0: all out) */
400	/* a frame streamed as it is made, for one too long to build first (a screen mirrored as it is drawn): begin, its bytes
401	 * F0 .. F7 in any number of puts, end. The ring is the stream's from begin to end (no other SysEx, no note out in
402	 * between: keep it short), each packet going in as soon as it is whole. A put waits while the ring is full and the
403	 * computer reads; one that waited PLAT_SYSEX_STALL_MS without a packet read gives up: the frame is cut there (the
404	 * computer drops a frame cut short at the next F0), the rest of its puts and its end return -1. Main loop; built for
405	 * an app with APP_SYSEX */
406	#define PLAT_SYSEX_STALL_MS 30u
407	int plat_sysex_begin(void);            /* 0 = the stream is open; -1 = no computer, or a send under way */
408	int plat_sysex_put(const uint8_t *p, uint32_t n);   /* 0 = in the ring (the last bytes held until more or end) */
409	int plat_sysex_end(void);              /* the last packet out, the ring free again: 0 = the frame went whole */
410	uint32_t plat_usb_session(void);       /* 0: no computer has set the FM-1 up; else a number that changes at every new
411	                                        * one (a bus reset, the cable out and in): what an app keeps for a connection
412	                                        * (a client's session) it drops when this changes */
413	/* the resource region (fm1.toml resources = FILE, FM1B_RES; app.h APP_RES_BASE, APP_RES_SECTORS: device/res.c):
414	 * the file's bytes read in place, *len their count; 0 (and *len 0) while the FM-1 does not hold this build's (not
415	 * yet written after an update, torn, another build's): the app does without. The host writes it
416	 * (tools/fm1_resources.py; the installer after an update); a sound reading it is stopped first (app_panic) */
417	const uint8_t *plat_res(uint32_t *len);
418

443	 * at, 0 muted .. 4096 as sent (the default; above is 4096), times MASTER. Muted, the FM-1 still takes the stream, so
444	 * the computer sees no change and turning it up again starts in step. The USB recording (usb_audio_in) is taken
445	 * before the computer's audio is mixed in, whatever this is: recording the FM-1 never records the computer's own

449	 * PLAT_USB_CH of them, beside the master on 1 and 2, as 16-bit samples (32767: the master's full scale, the render's
450	 * 1 << 22 at 4096). In app_render, the frame off frames into the block being rendered: its channels at p[0] ..
451	 * p[PLAT_USB_CH - 1], the next frame's PLAT_USB_CH_STRIDE on, for *run frames (where the ring wraps: ask again from
452	 * there). They start at 0 each block; the app adds into them, on either core (one writer a sample at a time), and the
453	 * platform sends them with the master's frames once app_render returns. NULL (*run 0) when no computer records (the
454	 * app then skips the work), and always with 2 channels; the host: a block's buffer, always taken */

```text
1	# The CPU: what we have seen it do
2	
3	## 64-bit multiplies among 16-bit loads
4	
5	On the FM-1 (AC79, pi32v2 at the boot loader's 360 MHz), code that inlines 32x32->64-bit multiplies
6	(`r9_r8 = r3 * r15 (s)`) among 16-bit loads (`r4 = h[r5+-380] (u)`) now and then leaves a register one bit off,
7	and the firmware crashes. The crash records show it plainly: a loop index of 0x12 read as 0x00800012, a counter of 0
8	as 0x00800000, `sp` a word off so that a return pops a neighbouring value. The memory the value came from is
9	intact.
10	
11	fm1-radio found it in PacketVideo's AAC decoder, which crashed every few minutes (October 2026). On the device:
12	
13	| Test (WiFi off) | Result |
14	| --- | --- |
15	| SBR's analysis filterbank alone, on fixed input, built at `-O2` | crashed within a minute, every time |
16	| the same, each run with interrupts off | crashed |
17	| the same without instruction pairing (`-mllvm -pi32v2-parallel-pack=false`) | crashed |
18	| the same with a `nop` after each multiply | crashed |
19	| the same with the multiplies in functions of their own (`noinline`) | 8 minutes clean |
20	| 1.2 billion 64-bit multiplies, each checked | no error |
21	| 2 billion 16-bit loads, each checked | no error |
22	| 16-bit loads beside 64-bit multiplies | crashed within a minute |
23	| 32-bit loads beside 64-bit multiplies | 2 errors in 4 billion |
24	| SYSVDD 13 (1.32 V) instead of 15 | crashed as fast |
25	
26	So keep 64-bit multiplies out of line in hot fixed-point loops: a helper marked `noinline`, as in
27	`int32_t mul_q31(int32_t a, int32_t b) { return (int32_t)(((int64_t)a * b) >> 31); }`. The helper uses the product
28	at once, so the multiply completes before any load that follows. In fm1-radio this cost the decoder about 50% of
29	its speed (7.8 ms a frame, was 5.1) and made it crash-free.
30	
31	Not known yet: which exact instruction pairs fail, whether the SDK's 320 MHz is clear of it, and how much other code
32	is exposed. Floating-point code (minimp3) has no 64-bit multiplies and never showed it. To look for it, list the
33	functions whose disassembly has `rN_rM = rA * rB` beside `h[...]` loads.
34
```
</details></tool-use>

````text
1	# fm1-base: design
2	
3	A base for M-VAVE FM-1 firmware, on felucca-bsp. A firmware is felucca-bsp (chip, board, update loader, packaging),
4	plus fm1-base (everything a firmware needs above the hardware), plus its own app. It is the platform layer that
5	FoMni-1, X0X, CTL-1 and the other firmwares share today, made into one maintained base.
6	
7	## Licence
8	
9	**Every file of fm1-base is MPL-2.0**, with a provenance that allows it:
10	
11	| Source | Why it may be MPL-2.0 |
12	| --- | --- |
13	| Leo Kuroshita's code from Felucca | his permission, recorded in hugelton/felucca-bsp#4; his name in `CREDITS.md` |
14	| Charles Vestal's code (the firmwares' platform layer: X0X, FoMni and the rest) | his own |
15	| keremimo's code | only what he has agreed to on the record (felucca-bsp#3; the second-core start once its PR has his comment; Melodee's code, 2026-10-31: LICENSING.md) |
16	
17	Nothing else goes in: no code by other Felucca contributors, no GPL code from anywhere. Every imported file's history
18	is checked first (its authors in git and, for files from Felucca, Felucca's README credits). Third-party material keeps its
19	own licence and is listed in `LICENSING.md`: the fonts (SIL OFL 1.1), JieLi's SDK files used by the build (Apache-2.0,
20	fetched, never committed).
21	
22	An app built on fm1-base may use any licence. MPL-2.0 applies file by file: changes to fm1-base's files are published
23	under MPL-2.0, the app's own files are the app's choice. A firmware that links JieLi's closed Bluetooth or Wi-Fi
24	libraries therefore has no GPL file in it at all.
25	
26	## Layers
27	
28	```
29	app (ui.c, project.c, dsp/ ...)            the firmware's own code, any licence
30	  |  plat.h (the platform interface)
31	fm1-base  device: plat_fm1.c, main_fm1.c, panel.c, lcd.c, gfx.c, storage.c, midi_uart.c, announce.c
32	          host:   plat_host.c (simulator, scripted), web/emu (the simulator in the browser)
33	          tools:  build.py, fonts, words, installer and site pages
34	felucca-bsp (git submodule, pinned)  chip/ boards/fm1/ loader/ tools/fm1pkg.py tools/fm1_install.py
35	```
36	
37	The app sees only `plat.h`. The device and the host implement it, so every app runs, unchanged, on the FM-1, in the
38	host simulator (tests, screenshots) and in the browser.
39	
40	## The platform interface
41	
42	`plat.h` is the union of what the 13 firmwares use today (68 functions), in groups. A firmware turns on the optional
43	groups it needs, and only those are compiled in.
44	
45	| Group | Functions (today's names) | Used by |
46	| --- | --- | --- |
47	| core | `plat_ms`, `plat_buttons`, `plat_keys`, `plat_enc`, `plat_master`, `plat_leds`, `plat_glow`, `plat_play_red`, `plat_keys_dim`, `plat_store_load/save`, `plat_cpu_pct`, `plat_xruns` | all |
48	| MIDI | `plat_midi_in` (USB or TRS), `plat_midi_out`, `plat_midi3`, `plat_sysex`, `plat_midi_out_room`, `plat_midi_out_link`, `plat_midi_dropped`, SysEx in (`plat_sysex_get/done/send`) | all; the extras by some |
49	| storage extras | `plat_store_load_prev`, `plat_store_head`, raw sectors (`plat_gal_*`) | X0X, SPH-16, XY-1, Polly, Mocky |
50	| second core | `plat_cpu2_*`, `plat_core` (fm1.toml `cpu2 = true`; how to use it: [docs/SECOND-CORE.md](docs/SECOND-CORE.md)) | LOOM-8; X0X, NuSaw and SPH-16 on their own copies |
51	| analog keys | `plat_analog_*`, `plat_cap_probe`, `plat_sense` | Velo, MONK-1, CTL-1 |
52	| profiling | `plat_cycles*`, `plat_stalls*`, `plat_cpu_peak_pct`, `plat_irq_stack_*`, `plat_ticks24` | X0X, SPH-16, XY-1 |
53	| power | `plat_battery`, `plat_battery_raw`; the supply rails are fm1-base's own, set at boot, with no call ([docs/SECOND-CORE.md](docs/SECOND-CORE.md#the-supplies)) | X0X, SPH-16, NuSaw, LOOM-8 |
54	| crash | `plat_last_crash` | X0X, SPH-16, NuSaw, XY-1 |
55	| Bluetooth | `plat_ble_*` | CTL-1 |
56	| concurrency | `plat_lock`, `plat_unlock`, `plat_yield`, `plat_idle` | CTL-1, Mocky |
57	
58	The names stay as they are, so moving a firmware is a change of include paths, not of code. A firmware's own oddities
59	(X0X's sample slots) stay in that firmware.
60	
61	The app provides the other side: `app_init`, `app_frame` (the UI, about 60 a second), `app_render` (the audio,
62	called by the platform's audio interrupt), `app_tick` (1 kHz, optional), `app_say` (the screen reader), and
63	`app_config`: the block size, the second core, the USB names, the store's objects.
64	
65	## Build
66	
67	One `tools/build.py` for every firmware, driven by the firmware's `fm1.toml`: the name, the package identity
68	(`FM-1_` + digits), the USB names (felucca-bsp's `FELUCCA_USB_MANUFACTURER` / `FELUCCA_USB_PRODUCT`), the app's
69	sources, the optional groups, the fonts. It builds the app and the update loader, checks the rules (no `double`, no
70	hardware access outside the BSP and fm1-base's device files), and packs the `.fwsc` with felucca-bsp's `fm1pkg.py`.
71	`tools/run_tests.sh` builds the host simulator and runs the app's scripted tests. The web pages (installer, emulator,
72	backup) are generated from templates with the firmware's name and words file.
73	
74	The FM-1 tells its identity to the update handshake (felucca-bsp `chip/ota.c`, cmd 0x11). M-VAVE's M-UPGRADE 3.11
75	takes `NAME_` and one to three digits only, so the plain handshake gets the name, `_` and the first three digits
76	(`FM-1_11000100` -> `FM-1_110`); the handshake with the one-byte body 01 gets the whole identity. The installers
77	(`tools/fm1_install.py`, `web/fm1ota.js`, the backup page) ask that way when the plain answer is `NAME_` and three
78	digits, and keep the plain answer when nothing answers (M-VAVE's firmware, the loaders, older builds). The scheme is
79	PERF-1's (deamonSLINKY/PERF-1), so its tools and ours read each other's firmwares.
80	
81	## What fm1-base ships
82	
83	- `template/`: a minimal firmware to copy: a screen with text, the keys playing a sine voice, MASTER as the volume,
84	  USB-MIDI in and out, a saved setting, the screen reader. It builds, installs, updates and runs in the simulator.
85	- `examples/`: one small program per subject: the screen and fonts, keys and LEDs, audio, MIDI over USB and TRS,
86	  storage, the second core, and later Bluetooth MIDI.
87	- `docs/`: the interface, the build, porting a firmware, the licence.
88	
89	## Order of work
90	
91	1. The repository: felucca-bsp as a submodule; FoMni's platform layer, the host simulator, the web emulator and the
92	   tools brought in, each file checked for its authors, MPL-2.0 headers, `CREDITS.md`, `LICENSING.md`.
93	2. The template, flashed and tested on an FM-1: boot, screen, keys, audio, MIDI, save, reboot, update over USB. This is
94	   also the device test of felucca-bsp's latest changes (the supplies, the second core held on reset, the USB names).
95	3. hwtest gets an update path from the template's hooks; the real hwtest is run on a device; the second-core PR is tested.
96	4. CTL-1 moves onto fm1-base, with its Bluetooth build, which can then be released.
97	5. The other firmwares, one at a time; the optional groups come in with the first firmware that needs each.
98	6. After CTL-1's move: a skill, "move a Felucca fork onto felucca-bsp and fm1-base", written from what that move took.
99
````
</details></tool-use>

**License:** The repository is under GPL-3.0. The page labels it "GPL-3.0 license" and shows a badge reading "License: GPLv3."

**Supported platforms:**
- **AVR:** ATmega328 boards (Uno, Nano), ATmega2560 (Mega 2560), and ATmega32U4 (Leonardo, CircuitPlayground)
- **ARM Cortex-M0:** SAMD (tested on Arduino Zero), Teensy, and Particle boards
- **ARM Cortex-M3:** BluePill, via two cores: Roger Clark's STM32F1 and ST's CMSIS-based stm32
- **ESP32:** Supported. The page says ESP8266 is "theoretical possible" but not implemented.

**Memory, RAM, and flash usage:**
- Program size for the VoltmeterSayQ example is about 21 kByte with the Roger Clark core and 32 kByte with the STM core.
- Enabling `NO_COMPATIBILITY_FOR_TONE_LIB_REQUIRED` can save up to 844 bytes of program size.
- `ENABLE_PITCH` adds around 160 bytes of program space.
- RAM usage is not stated.

**Sample rate:** 8 kHz. Timer 1 updates the voice output data at 8 kHz on all ATmegas, and `SAMPLE_RATE_DEFAULT` is 8000. The 8 kHz interrupt handling takes 8 µs on the Roger Clark core and 12 µs on the STM core.

**Frame rate and bits per frame:** Not stated.

**Vocabulary:** The page does not give a word count or file sizes. It points to the `Vocab_*.h` files in the `src` folder, especially `Vocab_US_Large.h`.

**Bytes per word:** Not stated.

**Encoder links:**
- python_wizard: https://github.com/ptwz/python_wizard
- BlueWizard: https://github.com/patrick99e99/BlueWizard (for Mac OS X)

The page quotes these as "To create LPC data you can use the python_wizard or the BlueWizard for Mac OS X." It also mentions Qboxpro, an old, unsupported Windows application.

```text
1	# felucca-bsp
2	
3	A base for custom firmware on M-VAVE synthesizers built around JieLi chips.
4	It holds the chip layer (clock, interrupts, flash, USB, UART, timers, boot entry) and one
5	directory of board code per device. It has no sound code and no user interface.
6	
7	Named after its first user, Felucca; it is not tied to that application.
8	
9	Unofficial. Not affiliated with or endorsed by M-VAVE or JieLi. Product and company names
10	belong to their owners.
11	
12	> **Experimental parts.** Some features here are **beta**: the second core (`chip/fm1_cpu1.*`), expanded flash
13	> (`chip/fm1_flash_ext.h`) and the cache RAM (`chip/fm1_cache_ram.h`). USB MIDI host is ported from Melodee, where input has run on hardware;
14	> this BSP port and its OUT path still need device validation. A higher clock remains a **concept**.
15	> What is established and what is not: [docs/EXPERIMENTAL.md](docs/EXPERIMENTAL.md). The safe test
16	> firmware (`examples/hwtest/hwtest.bin`) contains none of them. Bluetooth MIDI and WiFi, on JieLi's own
17	> radio libraries, are in [fm1-base](https://github.com/charlesvestal/fm1-base), which builds on this repository.
18	
19	> **Licences: settled.** The files here are MPL-2.0. Leo Kuroshita confirmed it for the Felucca code he owns
20	> ([#4](https://github.com/hugelton/felucca-bsp/issues/4)), and keremimo for his part of `chip/usb.c`
21	> ([#3](https://github.com/hugelton/felucca-bsp/pull/3)). Details in [LICENSING.md](LICENSING.md) and
22	> [NOTICE](NOTICE). The USB host port also has permission from Adrien Tibi (Recursive Field Instruments):
23	> [Melodee #75](https://github.com/keremimo/melodee/pull/75#issuecomment-6384184014).
24	
25	> **Licence notes before you start**
26	> - A fork of Felucca cannot move to MPL-2.0 by using this repository. To use another licence, start a new project and import this one: [Forks of Felucca](LICENSING.md#forks-of-felucca).
27	
28	> **Status: beta.** Split out of [Felucca](https://github.com/hugelton/Felucca). Firmware is built on it through
29	> [fm1-base](https://github.com/charlesvestal/fm1-base), and two firmwares are its proof points so far:
30	> [CTL-1](https://github.com/charlesvestal/fm1-ctl) (Bluetooth MIDI) and [Radio](https://github.com/charlesvestal/fm1-radio)
31	> (WiFi). Expect changes to file names and layout.
32	
33	## Devices
34	
35	| Device | Status |
36	| --- | --- |
37	| M-VAVE FM-1 | Supported. Used by Felucca. |
38	| M-VAVE Galaxia | Supported (board code: audio, knobs, switches, jacks, LED). Used by [GalaxiaSDK](https://github.com/dhilowitz/GalaxiaSDK). |
39	| M-VAVE Pocket AMP | Board code for audio, buttons and panel, checked on a unit. Used by [Pendel](https://github.com/hugelton/Pendel); its update loader stays in pendel-bsp. |
40	| M-VAVE SMK-37 Elite | Planned. Not started. |
41	| M-VAVE SMK-37 Pro | Planned. No board support yet. |
42	
43	"Planned" means the device is a target, not that it works. A device gets its own directory
44	under `boards/` once someone has it running. Pin maps and other board facts are added only
45	when they have been checked on a real unit.
46	
47	## Layout
48	
49	| Path | What |
50	| --- | --- |
51	| `chip/` | Registers, drivers and boot entry shared by the chip family; `libc.c` (the few routines a freestanding build needs); `ota.c` (the update session, which takes its hooks from the application); `fm1_perf.h` (cycle and stall counters) and `fm1_debug.h` (register access for development builds) |
52	| `chip/usb_host.c`, `chip/usb_host_desc.h` | Opt-in USB MIDI host: direct or one powered hub, MIDI input/output; [API and limits](docs/USB_HOST.md) |
53	| `chip/usb.c` | The USB device: MIDI, serial and audio classes (audio in, and with `FELUCCA_UAC_OUT` audio out) with the EP0 and poll code |
54	| `chip/fm1_sys.h`, `chip/fm1_guard.h` | Supply rails (VDC14 and SYSVDD at M-VAVE's levels), reboot and core reset; hardware guards (stack, write and fetch limits that end in the fault report), the stack floor, whether code runs in an interrupt |
55	| `loader/` | The update loader (builds as a RAM image; it includes `chip/usb.c`, `chip/ota.c` and `chip/libc.c`) |
56	| `boards/fm1/` | FM-1 wiring and drivers: ST7789 panel initialization and RGB565 transfers (`fm1_lcd.h`), key scan (with velocity and pressure from the keys, off by default: `fm1_input.h`), ADC channels, checked stereo Q23 audio DMA (`fm1_audio.h`), the headphone jack's switch (PB5: `fm1_jack.h`) |
57	| `boards/galaxia/` | Galaxia (a guitar pedal, board PD49 V03) wiring and drivers in one header, `gx_board.h`: the stereo converter on ALNK0 (44,118 Hz), six knobs including a nine-detent selector, two footswitches, the input jack detects, the two-colour LED |
58	| `boards/pocketamp/` | Pocket AMP audio input/output, buttons and panel. The board-specific update loader remains in [pendel-bsp](https://github.com/hugelton/pendel-bsp). |
59	| `docs/BOARD_IO.md` | Panel API, pixel byte order and lifetime; audio sample/rate guarantees, buffer validation, stop/restart and underrun behavior |
60	| `docs/EXPERIMENTAL.md` | Second core, expanded flash, USB host, clock: what is established and what is not |
61	| `docs/FLASH.md` | Application write regions, flash API, interrupt preservation, CPU1 coordination and verification |
62	| `docs/CPU.md` | What the CPU has been seen to do: 64-bit multiplies among 16-bit loads leave a register a bit off; keep them out of line |
63	| `tools/` | Package builder (`fm1pkg.py`), USB-MIDI installer (`fm1_install.py`), `fm1_rescue` and `get_sdk.sh` (JieLi's SDK, fetched and checked by hash) |
64	| `examples/hwtest/` | Test firmware for a real FM-1: screen, knob, buttons, LEDs, USB serial. `hwtest.bin` is the safe image; `hwtest-exp.bin` adds the experimental parts |
65	| `examples/felucca/` | Reference only: `ota_hw.c`, the hooks Felucca gives `ota.c`. Not built here |
66	
67	Headers include each other by file name. Build with `-Ichip -Iboards/fm1`. The loader builds from this tree with
68	the JieLi toolchain and gives the same image as it does inside Felucca.
69	
70	`tools/` has the package builder, the USB-MIDI installer and `fm1_rescue` (stock firmware back on an FM-1 that cannot
71	start, through the chip's update mode; macOS) (the loader marker `FELUCCA-LOADER-1` is part of the loader's contract). The loader, `ota.c` and `usb.c`
72	still use `FELUCCA_*` macro names; they will be renamed. `usb.c` needs `uac_fir.h` (generated by Felucca's tools) only
73	when its 48 kHz audio option is on.
74	
75	## Licence
76	
77	[MPL-2.0](LICENSE), applied per file: if you change a file from this repository and
78	distribute it, you publish your change to that file. Your own code on top of it may use any
79	licence. This repository can be combined with GPL code (no "Incompatible With Secondary
80	Licences" notice). See the notes at the top. Credits, including the JieLi SDK (Apache-2.0), are in [NOTICE](NOTICE).
81	
82	## Firmware that uses this base
83	
84	| Firmware | Device | Licence | About |
85	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
86	| [Felucca](https://github.com/hugelton/Felucca) | M-VAVE FM-1 | GPL-3.0-only | Multi-engine synthesizer firmware with a sequencer and a web editor. |
87	| [fm1-base](https://github.com/charlesvestal/fm1-base) | M-VAVE FM-1 | MPL-2.0 | A base and template for FM-1 firmware: platform, host simulator, browser emulator, Bluetooth MIDI, WiFi, USB audio. |
88	| [CTL-1](https://github.com/charlesvestal/fm1-ctl) | M-VAVE FM-1 | MPL-2.0 | A MIDI controller with velocity and aftertouch, scales and chords, an arpeggiator, a Euclidean drum sequencer and GM sounds; USB and Bluetooth MIDI. On fm1-base. |
89	| [Radio](https://github.com/charlesvestal/fm1-radio) | M-VAVE FM-1 | MPL-2.0 | An internet radio over WiFi: Radio Garden's stations, MP3 and HE-AAC, punch-in effects. On fm1-base. |

92	description. Rules are in [LISTING.md](LISTING.md).

94	## Contributing
95	
96	Issues and pull requests are welcome. By contributing you agree that your change is licensed

````text
1	# FM-1 panel and audio contracts
2	
3	Both drivers are header implementations. Include them in one translation unit,
4	like the other board headers, with `-Ichip -Iboards/fm1`. Initialize TIMER4 with
5	`fm1_time_init()` before either driver's startup delays. Applications serialize
6	access to each peripheral; neither driver supplies locks or a scheduler.
7	
8	## Panel: `boards/fm1/fm1_lcd.h`
9	
10	`fm1_lcd_init()` configures the SPI pins and the FM-1's ST7789 panel, waits for
11	reset and sleep-out, and selects RGB565, RGB colour order, IPS inversion and a
12	240 by 240 top-left coordinate space. The default SPI divider is 4. Its clock is
13	LSB / 5, so applications that change the system clock must account for that.
14	The original `fm1_lcd_hw.h` transport remains available for existing users.
15	
16	- `fm1_lcd_fill_rect(x, y, w, h, rgb)` fills a rectangle with a native RGB565 value:
17	  red is `0xF800`, green `0x07E0`, blue `0x001F`.
18	- `fm1_lcd_blit(x, y, w, h, pixels, pixel_count)` sends contiguous row-major
19	  `uint16_t` RGB565 pixels. `pixel_count` is the available source element count,
20	  at least `w * h`. No stride, clipping, scaling or colour conversion is implicit.
21	- Zero width or height succeeds without touching hardware or reading pixels.
22	  Nonempty rectangles must fit completely inside the display. Overflowing
23	  coordinates, out-of-bounds rectangles, null pixel pointers and short sources
24	  return `-2` before a transfer starts.
25	- Both calls block until completion. They stage one row in a 480-byte static
26	  buffer (a header static: one per translation unit that includes `fm1_lcd.h`), sending the high byte first. The source may be in RAM or XIP and may be
27	  reused when the call returns. Normal C pointer validity/alignment and the
28	  supplied source capacity are the caller's responsibility.
29	- `0` means success. A transport timeout returns `-1`, increments the existing
30	  `fm1_lcd_timeouts`, releases CS and switches SPI1 off (`fm1_lcd_spi_off()`).
31	  Reinitialize before retrying; the panel may contain a partial rectangle.
32	  `fm1_lcd_wait()` in the low-level transport now returns this status too, but
33	  leaves SPI1 on: existing callers that initialize once and ignore the result
34	  (fm1-base's `device/lcd.c`, `loader/ldr_screen.c`) keep drawing after a
35	  timeout, as before.
36	
37	Calls share staging RAM and SPI1. Do not call from nested interrupts or another
38	core while a transfer is active, or mix raw transport calls with panel operations
39	without the same serialization. The driver initializes the backlight on, as the
40	original transport did. `fm1_lcd_backlight(on)` still controls it; applications
41	using TIMER5 key scanning must protect this shared port-A read/modify/write
42	against that ISR, as documented in `fm1_lcd_hw.h`.
43	
44	## Audio: `boards/fm1/fm1_audio.h`
45	
46	### Fixed sample format and clock
47	
48	Every frame is two `int32_t` words in left, right order. Samples are signed Q23:
49	`-8388608` through `8388607`, sign-extended into the 32-bit container, with zero
50	for silence. The significant bits occupy bits 23:0, **not** bits 31:8. For
51	example, positive full scale is `0x007FFFFF`, negative full scale is `0xFF800000`.
52	A signed PCM16 sample becomes this format by multiplying by 256. Clip before
53	storing; the driver does not saturate, convert float/PCM16, or resample.
54	
55	The supported request is `FM1_AUDIO_RATE` (44100), the **nominal** 44.1 kHz family.
56	On the recognized stock audio PLL configuration, the hardware frame period is
57	544 ticks of the 24 MHz reference: `FM1_AUDIO_RATE_NUM / FM1_AUDIO_RATE_DEN`, or
58	about **44,117.647 Hz**, roughly +400 ppm relative to exact 44,100. Reference
59	oscillator tolerance applies too. A 256-frame half lasts about 5.803 ms.
60	Use this physical ratio for deadline calculations; nominal 44100 is appropriate
61	only when a protocol explicitly requires that advertised rate.
62	
63	This fixed-divider ratio was corroborated by prior FM-1 DMA-event measurements
64	against TIMER4 and USB frame timing; it is not a new physical measurement in
65	this change. The driver's fixed ALNK settings are preserved. Startup now rejects
66	unrecognized audio PLL register values (`0x119A0 != 0x45400203`, or
67	`0x119A4 & 0x07FFFFFF != 0x07503026`: its top bits are not compared, as
68	`fm1_clock_is_stock()` does not compare PLL1's) instead of promising a rate
69	under an unknown clock.
70	It configures the 44.1-family selector/dividers without retuning the shared PLL
71	or changing the CPU clock. Keep those PLL and ALNK clock settings unchanged
72	while running. Exact 44,100 Hz and 48 kHz are not supported contracts here.
73	JieLi describes the peripheral's channel, width and clock roles in its
74	[official IIS/ALNK documentation](https://doc.zh-jieli.com/AC79/zh-cn/release_v1.2.0/module_example/audio/iis.html).
75	
76	### Startup and buffer ownership
77	
78	Use the checked entry point for new applications:
79	
80	```c
81	#define HALF_WORDS (256u * FM1_AUDIO_CHANNELS)
82	static int32_t audio[2u * HALF_WORDS] __attribute__((aligned(4)));
83	extern void isr_alnk0(void); /* chip/fm1_isr.S -> application fm1_alnk0_irq */
84	
85	/* CPU0, global interrupts already disabled; TIMER4 and interrupt layer ready */
86	int rc = fm1_audio_init_checked(audio, sizeof audio / sizeof audio[0],
87	                                HALF_WORDS, FM1_AUDIO_RATE, isr_alnk0, 3);
88	/* Check rc before enabling global interrupts or assuming that audio runs. */
89	```
90	
91	`half_words` counts 32-bit sample words, **not bytes or stereo frames**. Each half
92	contains `half_words / 2` frames; the whole DMA span contains `2 * half_words`
93	words (`8 * half_words` bytes). Requirements:
94	
95	- Non-null, 4-byte-aligned buffer in ordinary FM-1 SRAM
96	  `[0x01C00000, 0x01C7FD50)`. The entire DMA span must fit below the reserved
97	  boot info, mailbox and vectors. Choose memory that does not overlap code,
98	  stacks or other application allocations.
99	- Nonzero, even `half_words`, no larger than 65534 (16-bit hardware LEN).
100	  The SRAM-span check further limits the usable size.
101	- `buffer_words >= 2 * half_words`, with actual allocated storage for that span.
102	  A C pointer does not reveal its allocation size: the caller must report its
103	  real capacity. Validation never probes or writes invalid addresses.
104	- A non-null assembly ISR wrapper and a priority in 0..7. The driver cannot
105	  distinguish a valid assembly wrapper from another non-null function pointer.
106	
107	Validation failures return `FM1_AUDIO_ERR_BUFFER`, `FM1_AUDIO_ERR_RATE`, or
108	`FM1_AUDIO_ERR_IRQ` before MMIO. A running DMA returns `FM1_AUDIO_ERR_BUSY`;
109	an unknown PLL returns `FM1_AUDIO_ERR_CLOCK`. Failures leave the registers,
110	interrupt configuration and sample data unchanged (register reads may occur).
111	On success, the driver masks the source, clears **both** DMA halves to silence,
112	resets ALNK, sets the address/length/format/clock, clears stale pending events,
113	attaches/unmasks the ISR and starts DMA. Call from CPU0 with global interrupts
114	disabled, outside the audio ISR, and enable interrupts promptly afterward.
115	Initialization takes about 10 ms of existing startup delays; it does not preserve
116	prefilled samples. Very small halves may already have pending events on return.
117	
118	The four-argument `fm1_audio_init(buf, half_words, isr, prio)` remains available
119	and now returns status. It assumes capacity of at least `2 * half_words` words
120	and uses `FM1_AUDIO_RATE`; it cannot detect a short allocation. Migrate to the
121	checked API and inspect the return value, including when an old caller previously
122	ignored the `void` result: a refused start leaves the FM-1 silent, with nothing
123	logged. `fm1_audio_init_checked` is declared `warn_unused_result`, so a caller
124	that drops its status gets a warning; the four-argument wrapper is not, so that
125	existing callers still build with `-Werror`. Code storing the old function type
126	must update it.
127	
128	### Refill, stop/restart and underruns
129	
130	In `fm1_alnk0_irq`, read `fm1_audio_pending()`, acknowledge auxiliary pending
131	bits with `fm1_audio_ack_aux(p)`, and service `FM1_AUDIO_HALF`:
132	
133	```c
134	uint8_t p = fm1_audio_pending();
135	fm1_audio_ack_aux(p);
136	if (p & FM1_AUDIO_HALF) {
137	    uint32_t half = fm1_audio_free_half();
138	    /* Fill audio + half * HALF_WORDS, exactly HALF_WORDS words. */
139	    render(audio + half * HALF_WORDS, HALF_WORDS / FM1_AUDIO_CHANNELS);
140	    fm1_audio_ack_half();
141	}
142	```
143	
144	The free-half number is a snapshot (0 or 1), valid only while DMA is consuming
145	the other half. Finish rendering within **one half-buffer period**, including
146	interrupt latency and higher-priority interrupts. Acknowledgement publishes
147	sample stores with `csync` and clears the half event; it does not pause DMA or
148	extend the deadline.
149	
150	Hardware continuously loops the two halves. If service is delayed, old data
151	plays again; a late write can overlap DMA reads and produce mixed old/new samples.
152	There is **no automatic silence, software underrun counter or queued callback**.
153	Pending bits can coalesce. Comparing the free-half snapshot before and after
154	rendering can detect some late refills, but misses an even number of transitions;
155	it cannot prove that no underrun occurred. Applications needing detection should
156	also measure elapsed time against the physical frame period and track ISR gaps.
157	On overload, shed work, produce silence **while the half is still free**, or stop
158	and restart. Do not zero an active DMA buffer from an unrelated context as a
159	recovery strategy.
160	
161	`fm1_audio_stop()` is repeatable and must run with global interrupts disabled,
162	serialized against the ISR. It masks the ALNK interrupt, disables DMA, clears
163	peripheral pending bits and drives the data GPIO low. It does not free, zero or
164	retain ownership of the application's allocation, install a new vector, or alter
165	global interrupt enable state. Do not manually unmask the old source to restart.
166	After stop returns, the buffer can be replaced/reused. Restart through either
167	init entry point: the selected buffer's two halves are cleared, DMA position is
168	reset and the new ISR is attached. Invalid restart arguments leave audio stopped.
169	This is a fresh start rather than sample-continuous resume. Stop/start electrical
170	transients and audible pop behavior require physical testing; PC6 is the I2S data
171	line, not a codec reset or mute pin.
172	
173	## Verification
174	
175	Run `tests/run_board_tests.sh` with a C compiler and AddressSanitizer/UBSan. The
176	panel fixture checks initialization, byte order, windows, a full frame, bounds
177	and failures at each transfer. The audio fixture checks parameter rejection,
178	SRAM boundaries and clocks. On Linux it also maps an SRAM-address buffer to test
179	successful startup, busy rejection, ISR helpers and restart with a different
180	buffer/size; other hosts explicitly report that fixture portion as skipped.
181	`tests/lcd_hw_test.c` checks the actual SPI completion and timeout handling.
182	
183	Build both hwtest images with `examples/hwtest/build.sh` and the JieLi toolchain.
184	Compile `tests/board_compile.c` with the same include paths to check audio and
185	pixel-transfer APIs against the target compiler as well. No tests flash hardware.
186	These checks do not establish electrical timing, colour order on a physical
187	panel, or audible restart/underrun behavior on a connected FM-1.
188
````

<summary>Tool use: **Read**</summary>
 `./third_party/fm1-base/bsp/docs/FLASH.md`

````text
1	# Flash access
2	
3	`chip/fm1_flash.h` provides runtime SPI NOR access. Its RAM routines temporarily
4	switch off the SFC/XIP mapping; normal firmware must use the `fl_*` wrappers.
5	The application must copy `.ram_text` into RAM before calling them, initialize
6	TIMER4, and provide RAM buffers. The example linker script and startup show this.
7	
8	## Configure an application's regions
9	
10	Define configuration before the first inclusion of `fm1_flash.h` (or
11	`fm1_clock.h`, which includes it):
12	
13	```c
14	/* All offsets are physical flash offsets; high bounds are exclusive. */
15	#define FM1_FLASH_WRITE_REGIONS(X) \
16	    X(0x97000u, 0xB0000u)          /* application data */
17	#include "fm1_flash.h"
18	```
19	
20	An erase must fit wholly within one region. A write is checked page by page
21	(each 256-byte page, or the part of it written, within one region), all before
22	the first page is programmed, so a write may run across regions that touch.
23	An empty `FM1_FLASH_WRITE_REGIONS(X)` allows reads only. Regions must be
24	constant expressions: no partition table or callback may be fetched from XIP
25	while it is disabled. The physical-capacity check always applies, including
26	when firmware supplies the older `FL_RANGE_OK(off, n)` override. If both are
27	specified, `FL_RANGE_OK` takes precedence.
28	
29	For source compatibility, omitting both selects the former Felucca layout:
30	
31	| Physical offsets | Existing use |
32	| --- | --- |
33	| `0x93000..0x97000` | Extra data |
34	| `0x97000..0xE0000` | Main store |
35	| `0xE0000..0xE5000` | OTA staging |
36	| `0xE5000..0xE7000` | Autosave |
37	| `0xE7000..0xFC000` | Extra data |
38	| `0xFC000..0xFF000` | Globals |
39	
40	The legacy `FL_DATA_*`, `FL_GLOB_*`, `FL_AUTO_*`, `FL_OTA_*`, `FL_XDATA*`,
41	`FL_STORE_OK` and `FL_XDATA_OK` names remain available in `fm1_flash_policy.h`.
42	They do not add write permissions when an application supplies its own policy.
43	
44	The updater has a separate write policy: application sectors
45	`0x4000..0x97000` and update records `0xE0000..0xFC000`. Changing runtime data
46	regions does not change what the updater overwrites or preserves. One more range
47	opens only when the package asks for it: a package with a `res.bin` entry (type
48	101, its flash address at byte `0x14` of the entry) has the loader write that
49	resource region after the app, in whole sectors of `0x97000..0xE0000`. The
50	loader leaves the region alone if any of its sectors starts with a saved
51	object's commit record ("X0X0"), and writes the region's own commit record
52	("RES1") last, only over a payload that matches its CRC-32. Its app image
53	ends below `0x93000`, but it can erase the rest of the containing application
54	window. In the extra-data regions, keep bytes `0xF00..0xF07` of every 4 KiB sector
55	erased (or unlike an update record): the loader searches there for records to
56	clear. Boot head, OTA layout and loader compatibility remain board contracts;
57	an application's region list must respect them.
58	
59	## API and errors
60	
61	| Function | Behavior |
62	| --- | --- |
63	| `fl_jedec()` | JEDEC ID; `0` if access is refused or the XIP mode is unsupported |
64	| `fl_status()` | SR1 and SR2; `UINT32_MAX` on refusal/unsupported mode |
65	| `fl_uid(dst)` | 16 UID bytes into RAM; enabled by defining `FL_UID` |
66	| `fl_read(off, dst, n)` | Raw physical bytes, including the boot head; 256-byte interrupt-masked chunks |
67	| `fl_write(off, src, n)` | Programs page-sized chunks; does not erase |
68	| `fl_erase4k(off, &took_us)` | Erases one aligned 4 KiB sector; timing destination must be in RAM |
69	| `fl_plain_window_init()` | Configures unencrypted XIP data reads and invalidates cached data; returns status |
70	| `fl_verify_xip(off, ref, n)` | Compares a mapped plain-data range against RAM; `0` on match, negative mismatch position otherwise |
71	
72	Integer operations return `0` on success. Errors are `FL_ERR_RANGE` (-1),
73	`FL_ERR_MODE` (-2), `FL_ERR_WEL` (-3), `FL_ERR_TIMEOUT` (-4), `FL_ERR_BUSY` (-5),
74	and `FL_ERR_BUFFER` (-6). Verification's historical negative mismatch result
75	shares the error-code space; use it as a success/failure check.
76	
77	The complete read/write range and buffer are checked before the first chunk.
78	Invalid ranges, arithmetic wraparound and buffers outside on-chip RAM are
79	rejected. A zero-length read/write returns `0` without checking its range or
80	buffer (`fl_write(off, NULL, 0)` as before); no flash transaction occurs. A later hardware failure or CPU1 job can still stop
81	a multi-page operation after earlier pages changed: these operations are not
82	atomic storage transactions. Applications retain responsibility for journals,
83	checksums and power-loss recovery of their own data.
84	
85	Every transaction saves and restores the caller's full ICFG value, including
86	when interrupts were already disabled. `irq_save` clears ICFG bits 8 and 9:
87	bit 8 alone (the SDK's `local_irq_save`) leaves priority-7 sources running, and
88	their handlers may fetch from XIP while it is off. `fl_plain_window_init()` follows the same
89	rule. Wrappers release the mask between chunks, allowing input/USB service.
90	Call these blocking APIs from the main loop, after arranging audio silence where
91	necessary; sector erase can take hundreds of milliseconds.
92	
93	## CPU1 and RAM-only execution
94	
95	The driver rejects access before changing SFC or flash pins unless:
96	
97	- The caller is CPU0 with global interrupts masked: ICFG bit 8 (`irq_save`, the
98	  SDK's `local_irq_save`) or bit 9 (`cli`) clear, as the SDK's `cpu_irq_disabled`.
99	- In a build with the second core (`FM1_CPU1`, defined before the first BSP
100	  header): CPU1 is held/off, or the BSP worker has acknowledged its RAM-only idle
101	  state. A build without it never starts CPU1 and does not check it.
102	
103	`fm1_cpu1_run()` revokes idle permission before publishing a job. The RAM worker
104	publishes idle after the job's final barrier and before publishing completion,
105	so a following dispatch cannot be overwritten by a late idle acknowledgement.
106	A busy or unknown worker causes `FL_ERR_BUSY`; the driver neither aborts a job
107	nor waits indefinitely. Arrange a job-free interval, then retry. The loader
108	holds CPU1 and clears ICFG bit 8 at entry, including when entered directly
109	through SPL/ROM.
110	
111	The BSP uses a single compilation unit. Include the flash driver, CPU1 worker
112	and stop helper in that same unit so they share their access state. Custom CPU1
113	workers are refused while running; they need an equivalent RAM-only idle
114	protocol before integration. The BSP worker leaves its interrupt bank disabled;
115	custom interrupts or DMA that fetch from flash must also be quiescent. Faults,
116	undocumented silicon behavior and failed flash hardware still require hardware
117	qualification; the software protocol does not establish those guarantees.
118	
119	Low-level `fl_*_ram` entry points remain for the RAM loader and established
120	callers. Their arguments/results must be in RAM, CPU0 IRQs must already be
121	masked, and calls from XIP must use `FL_FAR`. They apply the same CPU1 gate and
122	range/buffer checks as the wrappers. Never bypass the gate by calling `fl_enter`
123	or manipulating its state from application code.
124	
125	## Replacement flash parts
126	
127	`FM1_FLASH_SIZE` defaults to 1 MiB. For a physically verified replacement, set
128	its capacity (at most 16 MiB for the driver's three-byte addresses) and explicitly
129	grant its extra region with `FM1_FLASH_WRITE_REGIONS`. For example:
130	
131	```c
132	#define FM1_FLASH_SIZE 0x400000u
133	#define FM1_FLASH_WRITE_REGIONS(X) X(0x100000u, 0x400000u)
134	#include "fm1_flash.h"
135	```
136	
137	`fm1_flash_size_from_jedec()` in `fm1_flash_ext.h` can check the detected capacity
138	against the build's configuration before permitting writes. Discovery does not
139	automatically widen permissions. Vendor quad-enable handling and replacement
140	parts remain unqualified; this does not add four-byte addressing.
141	
142	Physical SPI capacity and mapped XIP capacity are separate. `FM1_FLASH_XIP_SIZE`
143	defaults to 1 MiB even on larger parts. Raw reads/programs work within the
144	configured physical capacity; cache invalidation is clipped to the declared
145	mapping. Do not increase the XIP limit without measuring the hardware mapping.
146	`FM1_FLASH_PLAIN_LO` and `FM1_FLASH_PLAIN_HI` select the unencrypted data window
147	(default `0x93000..0x100000`); they must exclude executable/encrypted content.
148	XIP verification is restricted to that declared window.
149	
150	## Verification
151	
152	```sh
153	tests/run_flash_tests.sh
154	JIELI_TOOLCHAIN=/path/to/toolchain python3 tests/check_flash_target.py
155	```
156	
157	Host tests exercise default/custom/read-only/loader/expanded policies, whole-range
158	rejection, page splitting, buffer bounds, nested interrupt restoration, busy CPU1
159	refusal, and error exits. The target check builds/links the safe and CPU1 examples,
160	fallback mode, an expanded-flash configuration with UID, and the loader. It
161	checks flash RAM routines for calls and direct branches into XIP and confirms
162	that the loader lives in RAM. These checks do not replace on-device erase/read/
163	write, interrupt-state and simultaneous audio/CPU1 validation.
164
````
